short: Three years of direct imperial government between two shogunates, and a comprehensive failure.
full:
With Kamakura destroyed in 1333, Go-Daigo returned to Kyoto and abolished the offices of shogun and regent, declaring that all land titles required his personal confirmation. The era name Kenmu was adopted in 1334. A records office and a court of complaints were set up to handle the resulting flood of claims, and the emperor issued judgements at a pace that produced contradictory grants and long delays.

The restoration alienated exactly the people who had made it possible. Warriors who had fought the Hōjō found land redistributed to courtiers and temples; a levy for a new palace was imposed on provinces already exhausted by the fighting. A satirical notice posted on the Nijō riverbank in 1334 listed the disorder of the capital in mocking detail. When Hōjō remnants rose in the east in 1335, Ashikaga Takauji marched out without imperial authorisation, defeated them, and kept the powers he had assumed. He took Kyoto in 1336 and had a rival emperor enthroned, founding the Ashikaga shogunate.
